They ship at the values the keyboard was measured with. Move one, glide a few sentences, and press the reset on the row if it was worse. Nothing here can break the keyboard.

Autocorrect
Fix typos automatically when you press space

When you press space, the keyboard compares the word you typed with the word list. If the word looks like a slip of a much more common word, the keyboard replaces it. The keyboard never corrects a word that you taught it. Autocorrect stays off in password fields.
Autocorrect confidence
How certain the keyboard must be before it corrects a word

The keyboard corrects a word only when the best candidate scores higher than the second candidate by this factor. A low value corrects more typos, but it guesses wrong more often. A high value corrects only when the word is almost certain. The keyboard always applies a correction that two sources agree on.
Context-aware suggestions
Reorder suggestions by the words around them

The keyboard reorders the top suggestions with the words you typed before them: your own word pairs, common English pairs, and words from the current conversation. The reorder applies only when there is real evidence, so the usual order stays for unfamiliar contexts. This never changes which word autocorrect applies.
Fix number row slips
Correct a stray digit to the letter below it

With the number row on, a tap meant for the top letter row can land on a digit, and "as3" appears instead of "ase". With this setting on, one digit inside a word can be corrected to the letter below it when you press space. The correction only ever swaps the digit for a letter. A word that starts with a digit, and a word with two or more digits, never change. This setting has an effect only while the number row is shown.
Add missing spaces
Split two words typed together when you press space

When the word you typed is unknown, but it divides into two words the keyboard knows, the keyboard can commit the two words with a space between them: "ofthe" becomes "of the". It does this only for a pair the keyboard has seen together, in the language\'s word pairs or twice in your own typing, and never for a word in your personal dictionary, so a name or term the word list lacks is not cut in two. A letter next to the spacebar can also stand in for the space itself, so "amibtomake" becomes "ami tomake", when that tap landed low on its key, toward the spacebar. The split applies only when no single word explains the typed text. Otherwise it stays a suggestion on the strip. Backspace right after the split puts your text back, like any other correction. With this setting off, the suggestion strip stops offering two-word splits as well.
Detect the language you type
Follow the language of the current message

When your languages share a keyboard, the words already in the text field show which language you write now. The keyboard leans its suggestions and autocorrect toward that language, and swings back when you switch. Type "ami tomake" on the English keyboard and it behaves like the Banglish one; type "how are you" and it behaves like English again. This works per text field and needs languages with "Also suggest from" set up, which romanized languages get automatically.
Detection strength

Gentle only reorders suggestions and never lets the detected language win over the keyboard\'s own. Balanced lets a clearly detected language take the lead, and autocorrect follows for all but the most common words. Aggressive hands over completely, so autocorrect fixes typos in the detected language even against very common words of the keyboard\'s own language.
Gentle
Balanced
Aggressive
Only reorders the suggestions. Your keyboard language always wins
A clear detection takes the lead, and autocorrect follows it
Autocorrect follows the detected language against common words too
Remember each app\'s language
Start from the language you usually write in this app

The keyboard keeps a tally, per app, of which of your languages the words you type there belong to. When you open a text field in that app, detection starts from that tally instead of from nothing, so a new message in a chat app you write Banglish in leans Banglish before you have typed a word, and a new email starts out English. The lean is worth about one typed word of evidence at most, so the first word you actually type outweighs it and a message in the other language is never fought. Apps with only a few dozen words of history lean less. The tally stays on this device and is wiped with the rest of the learned data.
Adaptive confidence
Correct less eagerly when you undo corrections often

The keyboard tracks how often you undo its corrections. When you undo corrections often, the keyboard raises the confidence it needs before it corrects a word. When you rarely undo corrections, the confidence returns to the value of the slider. The keyboard also remembers each correction you undo, one word pair at a time. "Remember my undos" sets how long that memory lasts.
Typing rhythm
Let your typing speed sway autocorrect

The keyboard measures how fast you type each word. When you type in a fast burst, typos are likely, so autocorrect fires more eagerly. When you type slowly and deliberately, for an unusual name or a word from another language, autocorrect holds back. The slider sets how strongly the rhythm sways the decision. Zero turns the signal off.
Adapt to app tone
Casual words rank higher in chats, lower in email

Chat words such as "lol" and "gonna" rank a little higher in messaging apps, and a little lower in email apps and email fields. This only reorders the suggestions. No word is ever hidden or blocked, and autocorrect does not change.
Undo autocorrect with backspace
Backspace right after a correction restores what you typed

Press backspace immediately after autocorrect changes a word. The keyboard puts your original spelling back and learns it, so it does not correct that word again. Turn this off to make backspace always delete one character.
Undo a correction from the strip
Show a chip that puts back the word you typed

Backspace undoes a correction only in the moment. Type one more letter and the correction is out of reach, and this is when you usually see it. With this on, the keyboard puts a chip at the start of the suggestion strip with your own spelling on it. Press the chip and the keyboard puts that word back, and learns not to make the same correction again. The chip appears between words and stands until you end the sentence. Not every correction gets one. The setting below says which corrections do.
How often to offer the undo
A higher setting puts the chip on more corrections

Most corrections need no undo. The keyboard was sure, the change was small, and you can see what happened. A chip after every one of those is clutter, and you learn to look past it. This setting sets the bar. The keyboard scores each correction on two things. The first is how sure the keyboard was. The second is how far the new word is from what you typed. A short word with one neighbouring letter changed scores high. A guess, or a word split in two, scores low. A correction that scores under this bar gets a chip. At the lowest setting almost no correction does. At the highest setting every correction does.
Remember my undos
How long a correction you undo stays undone

When you undo a correction, the keyboard remembers that exact pair of words and stops making the same correction. This setting says how long the keyboard keeps that memory. The keyboard reads an undo in two ways. Backspace, pressed right after the correction, is a clear undo. The keyboard also checks the text later, and counts it as an undo when your own spelling stands where the correction was. The second reading is weaker. You can go back to fix a typo by hand without seeing that the keyboard already fixed it, and type the same typo again. On every level except Strict, the keyboard ignores that second reading when your spelling is not a word it knows.
Off
The keyboard forgets the undo at once and corrects the word again next time
Light
A correction you undo needs much more confidence to apply again. The keyboard never stops it for good
Normal
One undo stops the correction for the rest of the message. Two stop it for good, and the keyboard asks you about it once more after a long quiet time
Strict
The first undo stops the correction for good, and the keyboard never asks about it again
Skip words in capital letters
Leave words typed in capital letters alone
Capitals from the word list
Write a word with the capital letter that its word list gives it

Some word lists spell words with a capital letter, such as the nouns in German and the names of places. When you type or swipe one of these words in small letters, the keyboard writes it with its capital letter. A word that the list also spells in small letters stays as you typed it. Backspace immediately after the word puts back what you typed. This uses the word list that you downloaded for the language. For the built-in English list, the keyboard carries the capitals of days, months, places, names and acronyms itself.
Correct the word before Enter
Enter corrects the last word, as space does

Enter ends a word the same way space does, so autocorrect can change the word before it. In a search box or a chat, Enter also sends the text, and you cannot see the correction before it goes. Turn this off to send the last word as you typed it. Space and punctuation still correct words.

You usually type acronyms, or words in capital letters for emphasis, on purpose. Examples: ASAP, OFC, NOOO. Autocorrect leaves every word in capital letters alone. Turn this off to correct these words like any other word.
Block offensive words
Keep profanity and slurs out of the suggestions

The keyboard does not offer offensive words in the suggestion strip. Autocorrect does not change a neutral typo into an offensive word. You can still type any word yourself. This setting only stops the suggestions.
Fix missing apostrophes
arent → aren\'t, im → I\'m, dont → don\'t

You type a contraction without its apostrophe (arent, isnt, youre, oclock…). When you press space, the keyboard puts the apostrophe back, and a lone \"i\" becomes \"I\". The keyboard leaves alone the words that are also real English words without the apostrophe (its, well, ill, shell…). This setting works even when autocorrect is off.
Automatic capital letters
Put a capital letter at the start of each sentence

Shift turns on by itself at the start of a text field, and after the punctuation that ends a sentence (. ! ? ।). This happens only in the fields that ask for sentence capitals, and only in the scripts that have capital letters, which are Latin, Cyrillic, Greek and Armenian. Nothing changes in Bengali or any other script without letter case. The keyboard never changes caps lock by itself.
Automatic space after punctuation
The keyboard adds a space after you type . , ? ! ; or :

You do not need to press space at the end of a clause: \"hello,\" becomes \"hello, \" by itself. A group of marks (\"...\", \"?!\") stays together. A mark typed straight after a number gets no space, so \"5,000\", \"3.14\" and \"5:00\" stay whole. If you press space yourself, the keyboard does not add a second space. Shift immediately after the space removes it. The keyboard leaves structured fields alone: passwords, email addresses, web addresses, number pads and phone pads. A space in these fields is a mistake.
Remove a space before punctuation
\"Hey .\" becomes \"Hey.\" when you type the mark

A space typed by mistake in front of a punctuation mark is removed when the mark lands. The mark must come after a word, a number or a closing bracket, so a mark at the start of a line is left alone. One backspace right after puts the space back. Languages that put a space in front of a mark on purpose, French among them, are handled by the setting below and are never hugged, whichever marks are listed here. The keyboard leaves structured fields alone: passwords, email addresses, web addresses, number pads and phone pads.
Marks that pull the space out
One character for each mark, with no spaces between them
Space before French punctuation
\"Bonjour!\" becomes \"Bonjour !\" in French and its neighbours

French keeps a space in front of the exclamation mark, the question mark, the semicolon, the colon and the closing guillemet, and one behind the opening guillemet, and so do Breton, Occitan, Walloon, Picard, Norman and Franco-Provençal. The keyboard types that space for you and stops every other rule from taking it back. It is a no-break space, so the mark can never wrap to the next line on its own. The mark must follow a word, a number or a closing bracket, so one at the start of a line is left alone. One backspace right after removes the space again. Every other language types exactly as before. The keyboard leaves structured fields alone: passwords, email addresses, web addresses, number pads and phone pads.
Space after a suggestion
Add a space when you select a word from the suggestion strip

This setting is on by default. When you press a suggestion, the keyboard types the word and a space after it, so the next word starts clean. Turn it off to type the word without the space. This helps in the languages or fields where a space after a word is usually wrong. If you go back to a word and continue it, the keyboard never adds a second space.
Wrap the selection with brackets
Press either half of ( ) [ ] { } < > \" \' or ` to put the pair around the selected text

When you select text and press a bracket, a brace or a quote key, the keyboard puts the pair around the selection. It does not replace the selection. Either half of the pair works. Example: select \"foo\", press ( or ) and you get \"(foo)\". The wrapped text stays selected, so you can wrap it again. Turn this off to make these keys always replace the selection, like any other character.
Close brackets for me
Press ( [ { and the keyboard types the closing half, with the cursor between them

This setting is off by default. With it on, pressing an opening bracket types the closing one behind the cursor and leaves the cursor between the two, so you type straight inside the pair: press ( and you get (), ready for what goes in it. Pressing the closing bracket when it is already the next character steps over it instead of typing a second one, and one backspace on an empty pair takes both halves out. The CJK brackets are included, and so are the fullwidth ones. Quotes are not: the apostrophe in \"don\'t\" shares that key, and closing it would be wrong more often than right. Nor is <, which outside code is a less-than sign. Passwords, web addresses and number pads are left alone.
Shift changes the case of the selection
Shift with text selected steps through lowercase, Title Case and UPPERCASE

When you select text and press shift, the keyboard changes the case of the selection. It does not arm shift for the next letter. Each press steps through lowercase, Title Case and UPPERCASE. Nothing changes for the scripts without case, such as Bengali. Turn this off to keep shift for the next character only, even while text is selected.
Suggestions
Show word predictions above the keyboard

The keyboard shows up to three candidates above the keys while you type: completions, corrections and next word predictions. The keyboard learns the predictions from your typing. Press a candidate to type it with a space after it.
Punctuation suggestions
Chips for . , ? ! and \' beside the word candidates

The keyboard adds a short row of common punctuation to the end of the suggestion strip while candidates show. A full stop or a comma is one press away, with no change to the symbols layout. A press acts the same as the key. When the keyboard offers an emoji prediction, the emoji takes the end of the strip instead.
Suggestions in every field
Show the suggestion strip even where an app asks to hide it

Some apps, such as Instagram and Google Keep, tell the keyboard to hide the suggestion strip on ordinary text fields. This setting is on by default, and the keyboard shows the strip anyway, as most keyboards do. Turn it off to follow the app and hide the strip. In the address bar of a browser it also lets the keyboard complete the words that you type, though it never autocorrects them there. Autocorrect, glide typing and Bengali (Avro) composing work either way, because they no longer depend on the strip. Password fields and number pads never show suggestions.
Suggestion strip always visible
Keep the suggestion strip visible before you type

Usually the top bar shows the toolbar, and it changes to suggestions only while candidates exist. With this setting on, the top bar shows the suggestion strip at rest, so next word predictions are always visible. The arrow on its left opens the toolbar when you need a tool.
Best suggestion in the middle
Show the best candidate in the middle slot

The best candidate, the one that autocorrect selects, goes in the middle of the strip. The second candidate goes on its left. Most keyboards use this layout. Turn this off to order the candidates from left to right.
Shorten long words
Where to cut a word that does not fit its slot

First, a long word gets smaller to fit its slot. If it is still too long, the keyboard removes some letters and shows an ellipsis (…) in their place. In the middle keeps the start and the end of the word, for example \"Punct…tion\". Most keyboards do this. At the end keeps only the start, for example \"Punctuat…\". This setting has no effect while Scroll the suggestions is on, because each word then keeps its full size.
In the middle
At the end
Suggest contact names
Complete names from your contacts as you type

The words in your contact names complete in the same way as the words in the word list. Example: \"was\" gives Wasi. The names also chain: after Wasi, the keyboard offers the family name. The keyboard reads the names into memory only. It stores nothing and sends nothing, and autocorrect never changes a name that it knows. This setting needs the Contacts permission.
Suggest contact emails
Complete the email address of a contact as you type it

Type the start of the email address of a contact, for example \"john\". The keyboard offers the full address (john.doe@gmail.com) in the suggestion strip. The keyboard reads the addresses into memory only. It stores nothing and sends nothing, and autocorrect never changes them. This setting needs the Contacts permission.
Contact emails in email fields too
Show them even where the app hides the suggestions
Remember email addresses you type
Offer them in the next email field

When you type an email address into a field that asks for an email address, the keyboard keeps it. The next time an email field opens, the addresses you used most show on the suggestion strip before you type, and typing the start of one narrows the list. It learns only from email fields, never from ordinary text. The addresses stay on this phone. To delete them, use Storage in the settings.

Email fields usually tell the keyboard to hide the suggestion strip. This would hide these completions where they help most. With this setting on, contact email completions still show in email fields. Other suggestions stay hidden there. Turn it off to follow the field, and complete email addresses only in ordinary text.
Suggest app names
Complete the names of installed apps as you type

The words in the names of your installed apps complete in the same way as the words in the word list. Example: \"sign\" gives Signal. Autocorrect never changes one. They rank below contact names, because ordinary words such as Files and Clock are also app names. The keyboard reads the names into memory only. It stores nothing and sends nothing, and it needs no permission.
Inline emoji search
Type \":\" and a word to find emoji, such as :smi for 😄

Type a colon at the start of a word to change the suggestion strip into an emoji search. \":cat\" offers 🐱, and a press replaces the text you typed. Press backspace over the colon to go back to normal word suggestions. Press space to keep the text exactly as you typed it.
Password manager suggestions
Show saved logins from your autofill service in the suggestion strip

When you select a login field, your password manager can offer saved entries as chips in the suggestion strip, instead of a separate popup. The password manager draws the chips itself. The keyboard gets only their size, and never sees the user name or the password inside them. The chips stay available in incognito mode, because they record nothing. This setting needs Android 11 or newer, and a password manager set as your system autofill service.
Smart replies
Let the system offer replies to the message you answer

Android System Intelligence can read the conversation on the screen and offer short answers, such as \"On my way!\". The answers show as chips beside the word suggestions, up to three at a time. The system draws them, not the keyboard. They come over the same channel as the password manager chips, but they count and switch apart from them. You can have saved logins in the suggestion strip without the system reading your messages, or the opposite. Incognito mode turns this off by itself. This setting needs Android 11 or newer, and only some apps offer replies.
Autopilot
Widen the touch area of the letters you type next
Only offer new words
Leave out the word you have already typed
Numbers from the letter keys
Type qwe with the number row off and the strip also offers 123

With the number row off, the top row of letters shows a small digit in each corner. When every letter of the word you are typing sits on one of those keys, the strip offers the number those digits spell in its last slot, beside the words, and one press types it. The word itself is never replaced without a press. Two or more letters are needed, so a single I or a single A stays a word. A number of five digits or more is grouped with separators when Group long numbers is on, using its grouping style. Nothing is offered while the number row is shown, since the digits are then on their own keys. This setting is off by default.

The suggestion strip normally keeps one slot for the word exactly as you typed it, which is how you keep a spelling the dictionary does not know. Turn this on and that slot is given to another suggestion instead, so all three offer something new. The cost is that a word the keyboard does not recognise has one fewer way to survive a correction, and the strip no longer shows you which candidate is the literal thing you wrote.
Words on the keys
Float the next word over the key that would reach it
Words on the keys
Float a predicted word over the key you would press next

The keyboard writes a small word above the key that would carry on the word you are typing. With \"hel\" typed, \"hello\" sits over the l, \"help\" over the p. Flick up on that key, or tap the word itself, and the whole word is written. After a space the keyboard offers whole next words above their first letters instead. The suggestion strip keeps working as before; this only adds to it. The BlackBerry Z10 typed this way, and it is what the Octopus keyboard copied.
Where the words sit
Above the key, in a lane of their own, or inside the key

Above the key puts each word in the gap over its key, half on the key and half above it, and the keyboard stays the same height. Own lane gives every row a strip of its own so nothing overlaps anything, and the keyboard grows a little taller. Inside the key writes the word over the letter, which never overlaps but leaves both very little room.
How many words
How many words may sit on the keys at once

At 3 or 4 only the words the keyboard is confident about appear, which is how the BlackBerry did it, and the board often stays empty. Higher values fill more keys, and past 9 the keyboard looks up a word for every key it can, which is how the Octopus keyboard did it. The board never shows a word it cannot fit; a key too narrow for the word is left bare.
What may appear
Which kinds of guess are allowed onto the keys

Completions carry on the word you are typing. Corrections fix it, and sit over the key where the word stops matching what you typed, so they are drawn in a different colour. Next words appear after a space, above their first letters, before you have typed anything. Turning all three off leaves the keys bare, the same as turning the whole feature off.
While gliding
What the keys carry while a swipe is being drawn

A stroke and a still finger want different things from the keys, so a glide has its own answer here and What may appear is left to say what a typed word may offer. Nothing keeps the board bare until you lift, which is what most glide typists want: mid-swipe a completion cannot be taken and a correction cannot be judged. Other readings floats the alternatives the keyboard is still holding, each above the key that reaches it, so you can steer to one. The next word offers what would follow the word you are drawing, above the key it starts with, so it can be flicked the moment the swipe ends. Whichever you choose, lifting your finger puts the next word on the keys as usual.
Completions
Corrections
Next words
Flick up to pick
A quick upward flick off a key writes its word

Flick up from a key carrying a word and the whole word is written. What counts is the direction, not the speed: the stroke has to go up, and go there fairly straight. A stroke that leans or curves is treated as the start of a glide instead. A flick that misses simply types the letter. With words on the keys turned on, a glide that begins straight upward off a key that is carrying one is harder to start; that is the trade.
Tap the word to pick
Tapping the small word itself writes it

Tap directly on a floating word to write it. This is easier to find than the flick, but the words are small targets. Words on the top row hang partly above the keyboard, and only the half over the key can be tapped; the flick works on all of them.
Flick sensitivity
How far off straight up a flick may lean and still pick

Each setting is a cone around straight up, and how straight the stroke has to be. Strict asks for an unmistakably vertical, unmistakably straight flick, which is what you want if you glide a lot and find your swipes being taken as picks. Relaxed accepts almost anything upward, for boards where the words matter more than the swipes. Balanced sits between them.
Word size
How large the floating words are drawn

A multiple of the size the small corner hints use. Larger words are easier to read but overlap their neighbours sooner, and a word that no longer fits over its key is dropped rather than shortened past reading.
Hide the corner hint
A key carrying a word drops its long-press hint

The small character in a key\'s top corner and a floating word are close enough together to read as one thing. With this on, a key showing a word hides its corner hint for as long as the word is there; keys with nothing to say keep theirs.
Long-press characters too
Allow words that need a long press to reach their next letter

Off by default. A word floating over a key promises that pressing that key writes the next part of it, and a character you can only reach by holding the key breaks that promise. Turning this on reaches more words, at the cost of some keys offering a word that a press alone will not finish. It changes nothing on an English QWERTY board, where the long-press characters are digits and accents that no English word uses: it is for a word like café or für on a board that keeps its accents behind a hold.
Autopilot
Quietly widen the touch area of letters you are likely to type next

As you type a word, the word list predicts the letters that come next. The keyboard makes the touch area of each key larger toward those letters. A press that lands just inside the key next to it still gives the letter you wanted, but only near the shared edge. The keyboard never changes a press in the middle of a key. This works on the letters layer only, and it needs Suggestions on.
Strength
How far a likely letter reaches over the key next to it

At 1 the keyboard changes a press only at the exact edge between two keys. At 10 a likely letter claims most of the space between itself and a letter that the word list does not expect. A letter never reaches more than one key width away, whatever you set here. 5 is the value the keyboard started with.
Show the effect
Draw a favoured letter at the size its touch area has grown to

The keyboard draws each expected letter over the board at the size autopilot gave it, so you can see what Strength does while you type. The keys themselves do not move, and you press them in the same places. At most three letters are drawn at a time, and they are the three the word list expects most. The drawing shows only while you type. It goes away during a glide, and it does not come back when you move the cursor into a word.
Size of the effect
How much bigger than life a favoured letter is drawn

×1.0 draws each touch area at its true size. A higher value multiplies the growth alone, so a letter that claimed no extra space stays the size of its key and only the difference gets larger. This changes the drawing and nothing else: your presses land in the same places at every value. The outline follows the same size, so the two always agree.
Outline the touch areas
Draw the boundary each expected letter has claimed

A thin line marks the edge each expected letter has grown to. Use it to tune Strength. The line traces the same edge that Show the effect draws, so the two always agree. The line is a tuning aid, so turn it off again when you are done.
Personal dictionary
Review, delete or add the words that the keyboard learned
Custom dictionaries
Import your own word lists for each language
Suggestion blacklist
Words to never suggest or autocorrect to
Smart chips
Answer sums, conversions and tool keywords in the suggestion strip

When a tool can answer the text you typed, the suggestion strip offers the answer instead of word candidates. Press the answer to type the result. Press the button on its right to open the full tool with the same numbers in it. The keyboard recognises everything on your device. It downloads only exchange rates, and only after you type an amount in a currency.
Calculate as you type
Convert currencies
\"150 usd\", \"150$\" or \"150 dollars\" offers the amount in %1$s
Convert units
\"1 ft\" offers the same length in metres
Tool keywords
Type \"wiki\" and the strip offers to open Wikipedia

Each tool has a few keywords. Type one keyword alone and the suggestion strip offers to open that tool and delete the word you typed. The settings of each tool list its keywords, where you can change them or clear them.
Resolve dates
\"next friday\" offers the date it lands on, and the calendar opened there
Answer weather questions
\"will it rain\" shows the forecast on the strip. Needs a weather location
Offer lookups
\"define serendipity\" offers the dictionary, \"who is Tesla\" offers Wikipedia
Translate hints
\"how do you say\" or \"in spanish\" offers the translator
GIFs for celebrations
\"happy birthday\" offers a matching GIF search
Group long numbers
Type 1234567 and the strip offers it grouped. One press types the grouped number

A number of five digits or more, typed on its own, is offered back with separators. Numbers that start with a zero are left alone, and so is anything joined to a letter, a dash or a slash, because those are phone numbers, dates and codes rather than amounts.
Grouping style
Where the separators fall
Automatic
Follow the language being typed: South Asian for Bangla, Hindi and the languages beside them, thousands everywhere else
Thousands
Groups of three: 1,234,567
Lakh and crore
Three digits, then twos: 12,34,567 and 1,00,000
The %1$s tool is off, so its chips do not show
The %1$s and %2$s tools are off, so their chips do not show
The %1$s tool is off, so these chips have no button to open it
One-time codes
Codes from notifications
When a verification code arrives in a notification, offer it above the keys. One press types it

The keyboard watches incoming notifications for a one-time code. When it finds one, a chip with the code and the name of the app that sent it appears above the keys. Press the chip to type the code. This needs notification access. The keyboard reads notifications on your device only, keeps the code in memory only, and sends nothing anywhere. Turn this off and the keyboard stops reading notifications at once.
Allow notification access
The chip cannot see codes arrive yet. Press to open the system switch
Only in code boxes
Show the chip only where the app asks for a code, rather than in every field

A code box usually asks for a number keypad, or names itself \"OTP\", \"PIN\" or \"verification code\". With this on, the chip shows there and nowhere else. Some apps give their code box neither, and the chip cannot find it — leave this off and a code is offered in any field while it is still valid.
Offer a code for
A code older than this stops being offered
Clear the notification
Dismiss the code\'s notification after the chip types it

A used code has no reason to stay in the shade. After the chip types the code, the keyboard dismisses the notification it came from. This uses the same notification access. Some apps post their code again after a dismissal; turn this off if that bothers you.
Type codes one character at a time
For the forms that give each character of a code its own box

Many apps and websites split a code across a row of small boxes, one character each, and move to the next box for you. A whole code sent at once goes into the first box, which keeps one character and drops the rest. With this on, the keyboard types the code character by character, so each box gets its own. This applies to codes from notifications and to codes pasted from the clipboard.
Glide typing
Swipe across the letters to type a word

Swipe your finger from letter to letter without a lift. The keyboard types the word when you lift your finger. Other readings show in the suggestion strip, so one press corrects a wrong guess. This works with every language when the layout has the letters to spell its common words. It stays off on a layout that converts what you type, such as the Chinese and Japanese ones.
Handwrite with swipes
Draw letters over the keys instead of glide typing

With Handwrite selected, the keyboard reads a swipe across the keys as handwriting. Draw a letter or a word. After a short pause the keyboard recognises it and types it, and offers other readings in the suggestion strip. This needs a handwriting model (Settings → Handwriting). A plain press still types its key.
Type words
Handwrite
A swipe across the keys spells one word
Draw a letter or a word over the keys. This needs a handwriting model
Glide across the spacebar
Swipe over the spacebar to continue with the next word

Keep your finger down. Glide a word, swipe across the spacebar, then glide the next word. Each crossing types the word and a space, so one stroke gives a full phrase. When this setting is off, a swipe across the spacebar makes one word.
Glide over Shift to capitalize
Draw through the Shift key mid-swipe for a capital letter

Gliding a name meant stopping to tap Shift first, which breaks the stroke. With this on, draw through the Shift key on your way and the word comes out capitalized; cross it twice and the whole word is in capitals. The key has to actually be crossed, and the walk out to it and back is cut from the path before the word is read, so the detour never adds a letter.
What a pass over Shift capitalizes
The whole word, or the letter you just left

Whole word: one pass capitalizes the word and a second pass makes it all capitals. One letter: each pass over Shift capitalizes the letter your finger came from, so a stroke can write HeLLo or LeanType, and ending the stroke on the Shift key makes the whole word capitals in one trip.

Ask when a glide is unclear
Hold your finger still to choose between the closest words

Some swipes have no single right answer. On a fixed Bengali layout the letters ক and খ share a key, so a word and its aspirated twin are drawn exactly the same way, and on any layout a hurried swipe can fit two words equally well. When that happens, keep your finger down and hold it still for a moment: the closest words appear just above your fingertip. Slide onto one and lift to type it. Lift without choosing and the keyboard types its best guess, as it always did, and the same words stay on the suggestion bar either way. Once the words appear the swipe is finished, so sliding to a word does not change it. Slide down away from the words and lift to type nothing at all. The settings below decide how sure the keyboard has to be, how long to hold, and how many words to offer.
When to ask
How close a call a swipe has to be before it asks

After a swipe the keyboard compares its two best readings. The closer they are, the less sure it is. Near ties asks only when the two words fit almost equally well. Close calls, the default, asks when the best word barely beats the next one. Any doubt asks whenever another word comes close. Every pause asks each time you hold still, whatever the keyboard thinks. The same words are on the suggestion bar either way.
Only when two words fit almost equally well
When the best word barely beats the next one
Whenever another word comes close
Every time you hold still, whatever the keyboard thinks
Time to hold still
How long to keep your finger still before the words appear

Hold your finger still for this long at the end of a swipe and the words appear. A short time answers faster but can open the words when you only paused to think in the middle of a word. A long time never opens them by accident but makes you wait. Small movements do not count: your finger can rest on the glass and drift a little.
Hold longer to always ask
A confident swipe still asks when you hold twice as long

When the keyboard is sure of a swipe it does not ask at the usual time. With this on, keep holding for twice the time and it asks anyway, so you can check any swipe before you lift. Turn it off and a swipe the keyboard is sure of never asks, however long you hold.
Words to choose from
How many words appear above your finger
Two to five words. Up to three fit in one row above your finger. Four or five use a second row above the first. More words give more choice, but each one is a smaller target to land on.
Learn my swipe style
Where your finger lands, how you draw each word, and which readings you correct

Nobody swipes through the exact middle of every key. A thumb cuts the far keys short and lands low on the near ones, and the keyboard used to charge every swipe for that. With this on, each swipe you keep records where your finger really passed each letter, and later swipes are read against keys moved to match. It keeps a few of your own shapes for each word you swipe and leave alone, so a word you have drawn before is read against the way you draw it as well as the textbook path. And it remembers when you take a different word off the strip, or backspace a swiped word straight away, so the same stroke reads your word first next time; only scrambled fingerprints of those words are kept, never the words. Backspacing a swiped word takes its lessons back. Turn this off to freeze what has been learned, or use Forget below to start over.
Forget my swipe style
Forget your swipe style?

Swipes go back to being read against the keys exactly as drawn, the shapes you draw words in and the readings you corrected are forgotten, and learning starts again from your next swipe. Learned words are not affected.
Words a glide can produce
Limit a glide to the most common words in your dictionary

A glide tells the keyboard which keys your finger went near, and in what order. Many words fit that loosely, so the keyboard uses word frequency to select one of them. A large dictionary holds many rare words, and a rare word whose shape fits a little better can win over the word you meant. This setting limits a glide to the most common words in the dictionary. It changes glide typing only. Suggestions, word completion and autocorrect still use every word, because the letters you type say much more than a swipe does. Words you teach the keyboard are never limited. The dictionary that comes with the keyboard is smaller than every limit here, so this setting does nothing until you download or import a large word list.
Whose words a glide can produce
Let glide typing lean on the words this keyboard has learned from you
Automatic is working like \"%1$s\" now. Pick any other option to start it over

A glide tells the keyboard which keys your finger went near, so what it competes against decides how often it is right. Most people write with a few thousand words, and once the keyboard has learned yours, the rest of the dictionary is mostly competition. \"Only my words\" removes it: glide typing answers with the words you have written, and nothing else. In testing that reads the words you write about five points more accurately, and it cannot produce a word you have never written at all. \"Prefer my words\" changes almost nothing on its own — it runs both and counts how often your own words were enough, which is what \"Automatic\" uses to decide. \"Automatic\" starts at \"Every word\" and asks you before it moves up. Picking any other option puts it back at the start, and while it is picked the line under this setting says which option it is working like. Whichever you pick, backspacing a glided word searches every word in the dictionary for the stroke you drew, so a word the keyboard has not learned is never out of reach.
Offer a full search while proofreading
Show a search button for reading the stroke against every word list when you tap back into a swiped word

When a glide produces the wrong word, the stroke you drew is the only record of what you meant — the letters left in the text are the keyboard\'s guess, not your finger\'s path. So the keyboard keeps the last dozen strokes of the field, and tapping back into one of those words can search its stroke against every word list you have, past whatever limit glide typing normally works under. That search is always available: hold a word on the suggestion strip and pick \"Search all words\". This setting adds a small search button to the suggestion strip that offers it without the hold. It is an icon rather than a sentence so the words beside it — the ones the search is offering to improve on — keep the room; hold the button to send it away. Whichever way you reach it, taking a word off the search fixes the text and teaches the keyboard that stroke, so the same swipe reads correctly next time.
Steadiness of the word while you glide
Stop the word changing under your finger on every small movement

While your finger is down the keyboard re-reads the stroke many times a second, and early in a stroke there is very little to go on — two letters in, a great many words still fit. Shown as they come, the suggestions, the word above your finger and the words on the keys all change several times per glide, which is hard to read and pulls your eyes off the keyboard. This setting makes the word already on screen hold its place unless another word is clearly better, and gives it a moment to itself before anything can replace it. A word that stops fitting your stroke is still replaced at once. Lifting your finger types the word you can see, so a steadier preview never means typing something you were not shown. \"Light\" is the default.
Finish long words early
Offer a word before you have glided all of it

A swipe is normally read from end to end: the keyboard matches the first letter to where you started and the last to where you stopped, so a long word cannot be offered until you have glided every letter of it. Tapping does not work that way — four letters into \"dictionary\" the word is already there. With this on, the keyboard may offer a word your stroke has only started, and lifting your finger types it. It only does so when that word is clearly a better answer than anything you have actually spelled, so it stays quiet on short words and on strokes that could be many things, and a word you have drawn in full keeps its place: \"thing\" glided to the g stays \"thing\", not \"things\". \"When sure\" is cautious; \"Eager\" offers a word as soon as it is ahead. Under \"Prefer my words\" and \"Only my words\" the early word is always one of your own, and the dictionary only reads a stroke you finish. Lifting on an early word is a choice, so the strip then offers that word\'s neighbours — its plural, possessive and the shorter word it ran past — instead of the stroke\'s other readings. Off by default. Not available on phonetic layouts such as Avro, where a stroke spells a romanization rather than the word itself.
Color the word a lift will type
Show when the keyboard is sure, not only which word leads

While you glide, the strip draws the leading word in bold. Bold only means that word is first, so a word the keyboard is sure of and a word it is guessing between look the same. This setting gives the sure word a color instead, which is the promise autocorrect already makes with the same color: lift now and this is what you get. \"When sure\" colors a word only when the keyboard is confident about letters you have not glided yet, so with \"Finish long words early\" set to \"Eager\" bold means ahead of what you drew and color means sure of it. \"Any early word\" colors every word that runs ahead of your stroke. \"Always\" colors the leading word of every glide. The color is the one set by \"Autocorrect word color\" in Appearance, so nothing changes until you pick one there.
Where the color shows
The suggestion strip, the word above your finger, or the words on the keys

The suggestion strip is where the autocorrect color already lives, so it always shows the color. The word pill rides above your fingertip and is what most people watch while they glide, so it carries the color as well by default. The words drawn on the keys can carry it too, which makes the whole board answer at a glance but is a lot of color at once.
Backspace removes a glided word
One backspace after a glide deletes the whole word

This setting is on by default. Right after you glide a word, one backspace deletes the whole word and its space, and the suggestion strip shows other words for the same glide. Turn this off to delete one letter at a time, as for a word you typed on the keys. Use this when your glides are usually correct except for one or two letters.
Space after a glided word
Add a space when you lift your finger at the end of a glide

This setting is on by default. The keyboard types a space after a glided word, so the next word does not join it. You can glide the next word, or type it on the keys. Type . , ? ! ; : or a closing bracket next, and the keyboard removes the space first. A press on the spacebar counts as the space that is already there. Backspace takes back the glided word and its space together. The keyboard adds no space in a password, an email address, a web address, a number pad or a phone pad.
Apostrophe in a glide
Glide through one key to put an apostrophe in the word

The letters have no apostrophe, so the keyboard cannot tell \"its\" from \"it\'s\" in a glide. Select a key here and that key means an apostrophe in a glide: swipe i, t, that key, then s, and you get \"it\'s\". The key still types its own character when you press it. Select one key only. Two keys make every word less accurate. This step is not necessary. A word you glide without it still works, and \"Fix missing apostrophes\" still repairs words such as \"dont\". The spacebar also ends a word in a glide, so \"Glide across the spacebar\" stops while you use the spacebar for the apostrophe.

Start error radius
How far the start of a glide can be from the first letter

Measured in key widths. The keyboard offers a word only when your finger went down this close to the first letter of that word. A high value lets a glide start off the key and still find the word. A low value refuses a glide that starts in the wrong place, which is stricter but can lose the word you wanted. Move this up if your glides start late or low.
End error radius
How far the end of a glide can be from the last letter

Measured in key widths. The keyboard offers a word only when you lifted your finger this close to the last letter of that word. The end of a glide is where a movement stops, so it is usually less accurate than the start. This is a separate value for that reason. Move it up if your glides slide past the last letter.
Path error radius
How far a glide can pass from a letter on the way

Measured in key widths. A letter is available to a word only when the glide passed this close to its key. A high value lets you cut corners and still get the letter. A low value keeps the keyboard to the keys you touched, which is faster and more exact, but a cut corner then loses the word. Move this up if long words come out with a letter missing.
Pause to mark a letter
How long to stay on a key to say the letter is in the word

A glide along one row of keys draws the same straight line for \"write\", \"wire\" and \"wrote\". Stop on a key for a moment to say that its letter is in the word, and the words without that letter lose. The stop counts for the key you stop on, not for the keys next to it. A stop does not write a letter twice: draw a loop for that. The value is a multiple of your own speed in that same glide, not a number of seconds, so it works in a quick glide and a slow one alike. A low value accepts a short stop, but a careful glide that slows down everywhere then marks keys that it only goes past. A high value asks for a clear stop.
Loop to double a letter
Draw a small circle on a key to write the letter twice

This is the mark Swype taught, and it is the only mark that writes a letter twice. Glide to the letter, go around on it one time, and carry on. The circle costs the word nothing, because the keyboard takes the loop out of the distance your finger travelled. The circle belongs to the one key nearest its middle, so the keys that its edge goes over stay out of the word. Turn this off if your glides curl on the way and you get letters written twice that you did not ask for.
Loop sensitivity
How much of a circle a curl must be to count as one

Measured in key widths of drawn path. A low value reads a small curl as a mark, which is less work to draw but also catches the shake of a slow turn. A high value asks for a circle you drew on purpose.
Biggest loop that counts
Wider circles are a path through keys, not a mark on one

Measured in key widths. A mark has to be small enough to sit on one key. A word such as \"murderer\" goes around a ring of keys next to each other and draws a wide circle that means nothing of the sort, so keep this under the width of one key. A low value counts only a tight circle and keeps the letters around it out of it.
Loop centring
How near the letter the middle of a circle must be

Measured in key widths. The keyboard gives a circle to the one key nearest its middle, and only if that key is this near. A circle drawn through a key sits about a third of a key to one side, so a very low value finds no letter for it and the mark does nothing. A high value also accepts a circle drawn between two keys, and gives it to the nearer one.
Wiggle to mark a letter
Rub back and forth on a key to say the letter is in the word

The moving way to do what a pause does: instead of a stop, scrub over the key. It says that the letter is in the word. It does not write the letter twice. This is off, because a slow turn drawn with an unsteady finger looks much the same, and the keyboard then marks keys that you only went past. Turn it on if this is the mark you make.
Wiggle strength
How much a rub counts, compared with a full stop
A value of 100 percent makes a rub as strong as a full stop on the key. A lower value leaves it as a hint, which a much more common word can still win against. Used only while the switch above is on.
Biggest wiggle that counts
How far the finger can go in a rub
Shapes kept per word
How many ways of swiping one word are remembered

Learn my swipe style keeps your own shapes for each word you swipe, and a swipe is read against the nearest of them. Swipe a word the same way and the shape settles in; swipe it a clearly different way and that is kept as another shape, up to this many, the least used making room. Raise it if you swipe some words several different ways and the keyboard keeps forgetting one of them. The shapes travel in a backup under Swipe style, so you can see how many your words really use. Lowering it takes the extras out of use at once, and they are only deleted when that word next learns a new shape. Used only while Learn my swipe style is on.
Measured in key widths. Keep this under the width of one key, or a word that goes from one key to the key next door and back reads as a rub on one key. Used only while the switch above is on.
Swipe start distance
How far to move before a glide starts. A low value is more sensitive

This is the finger movement that changes a press into a glide. It is a multiple of the system touch slop. A low value starts the glide sooner and is more sensitive, but a still press can start a glide. A high value needs a more deliberate swipe.
Delay after typing
Resist the start of a glide immediately after a press

Immediately after you press a key, a small movement off the key can look like a glide. In this window a glide must travel further before it starts, and the extra distance decreases across the window. Fast typing stays clean, and a deliberate swipe still starts. A high value stops more accidents, but a glide immediately after typing starts more slowly. 0 turns this off.
Extra time for a dot or a cross
Time to add a dot or a cross before the press types a letter

Letters such as i, j and t need a separate mark after the main stroke. For this time after you draw a stroke, a press over the letters becomes another stroke of the same character, the dot or the cross. It does not type that key. A press after the window types as usual. 0 turns this off.
Trail width
Thickness of the glide trail
Trail length
How long the trail stays behind your finger
Word preview
Float the word above your finger as you glide

While you glide, the word that the keyboard reads so far floats above your finger, and it changes as you go. Turn this off and the word appears only on the suggestion strip.\n\nThis does not change what a glide types.
Preview distance above finger
How far above your finger the word floats

Your hand covers more of the screen than your fingertip does, so the word can end up behind it. Raise this until you can read the word while you glide.\n\nThe word is drawn inside the keyboard. Near the top row, a large distance stops at the top edge.
Preview sideways shift
Move the word left or right of your finger

Your hand covers one side of your finger more than the other. Move the word to the other side and you can read it without moving your hand.\n\nA negative value moves it to the left. A positive value moves it to the right. Near the edge of the keyboard the word stops at the edge.

Size of the word that floats above your finger
This is the size of the text in the floating word only. The suggestion strip and the keys do not change.
Preview color
Background behind the floating word
By default the floating word takes its color from the keyboard theme, which is the same color as the key popup. Pick a color here and it uses that instead. Reset the row to follow the theme again.
Preview text color
Color of the floating word itself
By default the floating word takes its text color from the keyboard theme. Pick a color here and it uses that instead. Reset the row to follow the theme again.
One word on the strip
While you glide, show only the current word

While you glide, the suggestion strip shows every word that fits your stroke, and the words change as you move. Turn this on and the strip shows only the word that the keyboard reads now.\n\nThe other words come back on the strip when you lift your finger. If the ambiguity picker is on, it still offers them during the stroke. This does not change what a glide types.

Quick swipe on the spacebar
A swipe that starts to move immediately

Swipe left or right on the spacebar without a pause. \"Language\" steps through your input modes, with a live preview above the spacebar. Lift your finger to switch. Press and hold the spacebar to show the picker before you swipe. That only works while \"Press and hold, then swipe\" is set to the language or to nothing, because that setting owns the hold. \"Cursor\" moves the text cursor one character for each step. A press without movement always types a space.
Press and hold, then swipe
Press and hold the spacebar, then swipe

Press and hold the spacebar past the hold delay, then swipe. This gives the spacebar a second, separate swipe action. Example: a quick swipe switches the language, and a press and hold with a swipe moves the cursor. You can also set both to the same action. Anything but the language here takes the hold for itself, so holding the spacebar stops opening the language picker. The picker stays on the globe key and on the quick swipe.
2-D cursor touchpad
The cursor swipe also moves up and down

This setting changes the spacebar cursor swipe into a touchpad. The cursor moves left and right, and a swipe up or down moves the cursor between lines. This applies only to the swipe actions set to \"Cursor\" above.
The swipe does nothing
Change to your next language

Open the number pad
Open the Android list of keyboards, to change to a different keyboard app. On the press and hold setting, the hold alone opens it.
Swipe in from the edge to go back
A swipe in from the left or right edge of the keyboard closes a panel or the keyboard

Some phones do not let the back gesture of the system start over the keyboard, so you must start it above the keyboard. With this setting on, a swipe that starts at the left or right edge of the keyboard and moves in does the same thing. It closes the panel that is open, for example the voice panel, which also stops the recording. When no panel is open, it closes the keyboard. This setting is off by default, because a glide that starts at the very edge and moves in looks the same. Start glides a little in from the edge.
Swipe down to hide the keyboard
A swipe down on the spacebar closes the keyboard

Swipe straight down on the spacebar to close the keyboard. This setting is off by default, so an accidental swipe down never closes the keyboard. When the 2-D cursor touchpad is on, a swipe down moves the cursor instead. The touchpad has priority.
Swipe down to type the hint
A quick swipe down on a key types its small corner character

Each key shows its first press-and-hold character in the corner, such as 1 on q. A short, quick swipe straight down on the key types that character with no hold. This works on any key that has press-and-hold characters, on every layer. The spacebar, backspace and the shift and modifier keys keep their own swipes. The swipe must be short, straight down and fast. A longer or slower drag is a glide, as before. With glide typing on, a very fast glide of a short word that goes straight down, such as \"ed\", can type the hint instead. This setting is off by default.
Swipe up for a capital
A quick swipe up on a letter types it as a capital

A short, quick swipe straight up on a letter types its capital, with no need to press shift first. On a key that has its own shifted character, such as a number key with a symbol above it, the swipe types that character. The swipe must be short, straight up and fast, like the swipe down for the hint. A longer or slower drag is a glide, as before. If Words on the keys shows a word on the key, a swipe up still takes that word. With glide typing on, a very fast glide of a short word that goes straight up, such as \"de\", can type a capital instead. This setting is off by default.
Spacebar long press keys

Type the characters you want on the spacebar long press, with a space between each one. Example: 🙂 ❤️ 👍. The keyboard then shows them in a popup when you press and hold the spacebar. Leave this blank to keep the normal long press, which opens the language picker or repeats spaces.

Swipe on forward delete
Swipe right on the forward delete key to clear the text ahead

Press the forward delete key and swipe right. Each step of the swipe deletes one more word, or one more character, ahead of the cursor.
