Shift and Enter type a new line
Add a line break in a chat app instead of sending the message

Chat and search fields tell the keyboard that Enter means Send, Go or Search. Usually you cannot put a line break in a message without sending it. With this setting on, press shift first, or hold shift on a physical keyboard, and Enter types a real new line. The Enter key shows the new line symbol while shift is armed, so you can see the result before you press it.

Shift stays armed for as long as you leave it up, so a message can run to as many lines as you like. It comes back down when you type a letter or press shift again.

Only a shift that you press yourself counts. The keyboard ignores the shift that automatic capital letters arms at the start of a message, so the first line of a message still sends. The keyboard also ignores caps lock.

Turn it off to follow the Enter action of the app whatever shift is doing.
Volume keys move the cursor
Volume up and volume down move the text cursor

While the keyboard is open, volume down moves the cursor one character left, and volume up moves it one character right. Press and hold a key to repeat. Everywhere else, and as soon as the keyboard closes, the volume keys work as usual.
Release the keys while audio plays
Keep the volume control while something plays

While music, a video or a podcast plays, the volume keys change the volume again, even with the keyboard open. You can always turn the sound down while you type a reply. Cursor control comes back when the audio stops.\n\nTurn this off to make the volume keys always move the cursor while the keyboard shows.
Process the physical keys
Transliterate, correct and suggest as you type on a physical keyboard

With a physical keyboard connected, the keys go through the same engine as the on-screen keyboard. Phonetic layouts transliterate, so "ami" gives "আমি". Words compose for suggestions, and autocorrect runs when you press space. The word you type shows with an underline in the field until you finish it.

Shortcuts (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Z), the arrow keys, the function keys and everything in password fields always go straight to the app, at any setting.

Turn this off to type the raw characters straight into the field. The layout of the physical keyboard then controls the input.
Tool shortcuts
Open tools from a physical keyboard without touching the screen

Press the shortcut key. Each button on the keyboard then shows the key that operates it: a number under each toolbar icon, a letter under each tool in the toolbox, and Shift with a key for the symbol and emoji rows.

T opens the full toolbox, and ? shows the list of every key, including the tools that are not on the screen.

The shortcut key is two presses of Ctrl by default. No app uses this, because a Ctrl alone makes no character, and the keyboard still passes it through. You can change the shortcut key and every letter below.
Ctrl + number opens a toolbar tool
Ctrl+1 opens the toolbox, Ctrl+2 the first tool, and so on

The numbers count the buttons on the toolbar from the start. Ctrl+1 is the toolbox button, Ctrl+2 is the first tool after it. Ctrl+0 is the tenth button.

This needs no shortcut key first. Turn it off if you use Ctrl with a number in your apps: browsers and editors change tab with it, and the keyboard takes the key first while you write in a text field.

The same numbers also work after the shortcut key, at any setting.
Write the modifier names
Show Ctrl and Shift on the keys instead of their symbols

The keys under each button read \"Ctrl+2\" and \"Shift+Q\". These are the names printed on a PC keyboard.\n\nTurn this off for the shorter symbols. They take less space, but they come from Mac keyboards, and a keyboard that does not print them gives you no help to read them.
Time to press a key
How long the keys stay on the screen after the shortcut key

After you press the shortcut key, each button shows the key that operates it. This is how long they stay before the keyboard goes back to usual.\n\nMake this longer while you learn the keys. Make it shorter when you know them, because the keyboard does nothing else until the time is finished or you press a key.
%1$ss
Show the suggestion numbers
Put the key under each suggestion while a physical keyboard is connected

Each suggestion shows the key that selects it, for as long as a physical keyboard is connected.\n\nThis applies only to \"Alt + number\", which needs no shortcut key first. With \"After the shortcut key\", the numbers show after you press the shortcut key, because that is when they operate.
macOS shortcuts
Command and Option behave as they do on a Mac

For a keyboard made for a Mac. Command is the key next to the space bar.

Command+C, Command+V, Command+X and Command+A copy, paste, cut and select all. Command+Z is undo and Command+Shift+Z is redo. Command+Left and Command+Right go to the start and the end of the line. Option+Left and Option+Right move one word. Option+Backspace deletes one word, and Command+Backspace deletes to the start of the line. Hold Shift with a move to select.

Ctrl keeps its usual behaviour, and every other Command shortcut goes to the app. Some devices keep a small number of Command shortcuts for the system, and those do not reach the keyboard.
Ctrl+Space changes the language
Hold Ctrl to browse the language list, release to switch

Ctrl+Space goes to the next language and Ctrl+Shift+Space to the one before. Keep Ctrl held and press Space again to step through the list on screen. The keyboard switches when Ctrl comes back up. Esc cancels.

Some apps use Ctrl+Space themselves, for example code editors use it to show completions. While this is on, the keyboard takes the shortcut when you type in those apps. Turn it off here to give it back.

If the shortcut key that opens tools is also set to Ctrl+Space, the language switch wins. A keyboard with its own language key does not need this setting: that key always works.
Tool shortcuts list
Which letter opens which tool
Arrow keys move a highlight
Arrows move a highlight in a tool, Enter selects it, Esc closes the tool

In a tool, the arrow keys move a highlight over the emoji, the clips or the results. Enter uses the item with the highlight. Tab moves between the search box, the category chips and the results.\n\nThe highlight shows only after you press a key. It never shows while you use the keyboard by touch.
Arrow keys move over the keys
A ring on one key; the centre button or Enter types it

For a television remote, which has no other way to reach a key. The arrow keys move a ring from key to key and the centre button types the key it is on. Left and right stay inside the row. Up from the top row leaves the keyboard, so the remote can go back to the app.

Hold the centre button to open the alternates of the key the ring is on, then pick one with the arrows. Escape puts the ring away, so Enter goes back to the text field.

On a television this is on to begin with. Everywhere else it starts off, because the arrow keys belong to the text field you are typing in.
Esc closes the tool
Escape closes an open tool instead of going to the app
Escape closes only what the keyboard has open. With no tool open, Escape goes straight to the app, so it still stops a page load or exits insert mode in an editor.
Number keys select suggestions
Type a suggestion by its number in the suggestion strip
The number keys type numbers only
The safe choice. Nothing else uses the shortcut key
One key less, but many apps use Alt with a number for their tabs

You cannot press the suggestion strip while you type on a physical keyboard. A number key selects a suggestion instead.\n\n\"After the shortcut key\" is the safe choice, because nothing else uses it. \"Alt + number\" needs one key less, but browsers, editors and chat apps use a modifier with a number to switch tabs and workspaces.
Show the keyboard for shortcuts
A shortcut that opens a tool also shows the keyboard

With a physical keyboard, there is usually no on-screen keyboard, and a tool has no space to draw. With this setting on, a shortcut that opens a tool shows the keyboard. When you close the tool, the keyboard hides again.
Punctuation marks
One mark per character, in the order you want them. Leave empty for . , ? ! \'
Swipe down for more suggestions
Swipe down on the suggestions to see every word the keyboard ranked

The strip shows only a few words. With this on, swipe down on it while it has words and a grid of up to 24 suggestions covers the keys, best first. Tap one to use it, or swipe the strip again or tap Back to the keys to close the grid. When this is on, a downward swipe over suggestions opens the grid instead of hiding the keyboard; over an empty strip it still hides it if that setting is on. This setting is off by default.
Number of suggestions
How many words the suggestion strip shows at once

The strip splits its width evenly between the suggestions, so more of them means each one is narrower and long words are shrunk further to fit. Three suits a phone. A tablet or a landscape screen has room for more. This setting is 3 by default.
Emoji takes a slot
Count a suggested emoji as one of the suggestions
Keep suggestions in place
Same-width slots, and the best word never moves

Normally the words share the strip between them: two words split it in half, and an emoji, a row of punctuation marks or a tool\'s chip pushes the words aside to make room. With this setting on, the strip is always cut into the number of suggestions, every slot the same width, and a slot with nothing to show stays empty. The best word keeps the slot it always has. Anything that is not a word takes a slot of its own: a suggested emoji or the punctuation marks the last slot, a tool\'s keyword chip the first. This setting is off by default.
Coloured suggestions
Put each word on a pill of the theme\'s accent colour

Each suggestion sits on a rounded pill in the theme\'s accent colour, with the best word\'s pill the deepest, so the slots are told apart by colour rather than by thin dividers. With a Material You theme the colour follows your wallpaper. This setting is off by default.
Suggested emoji
How many emoji ride after the words

How many suggested emoji can follow the words on the strip, from one to four. Four is the default. While an emoji takes a slot, the slot holds one, whatever this says. Emoji suggestions are turned on and off under Emoji.

Suggested emoji normally ride after the words, up to four of them, on top of the number of suggestions. With this setting on, the best emoji takes the last slot and the words get one fewer, so the strip never shows more than the number of suggestions. Emoji suggestions are turned on and off under Emoji. This setting is off by default.
Scroll the suggestions
Show each word at full size, and every word found, in a strip that scrolls sideways

Normally the strip splits its width evenly and shrinks long words to fit their slot. With this on, every word keeps its natural size and the strip scrolls sideways instead. The strip also carries on past the number of suggestions, through every word the keyboard found, so the one you want is a swipe away even when it ranked fourth or tenth. Short words still fill the visible part as before. Turn it on if you want five or six suggestions on a narrow phone, or if your word is often not among the first few. This setting is off by default.
Double space
What two quick presses of space type

Press space two times quickly at the end of a word. Full stop replaces the first space with a full stop, so you can end a sentence with no change to the symbols layout. Tab replaces it with a tab character, which helps with indents and forms. Two spaces leaves both spaces as they are.
Two spaces
Full stop
Tab
Two presses type two spaces
The first space becomes a full stop
The first space becomes a tab character
Double space speed
How quickly the two spaces have to follow each other

Two spaces closer together than this count as a double space and become a full stop or a tab. Raise it if you type slowly and never get the full stop. Lower it if you get full stops you did not mean. This setting is 400 ms by default.
Cursor speed
How far you slide along the spacebar to move one character
Keep moving while held
A cursor swipe held still, or past the end of the spacebar, keeps going

The spacebar is shorter than a long line of text. With this setting on, a cursor swipe keeps going by itself, about eight characters a second: at once when your finger is past either end of the spacebar, and after a short pause when you hold your finger still away from where the swipe began. Move your finger again, or lift it, to stop. Short swipes and fine adjustments near where you started are not affected. This setting is off by default.
Whole keyboard as touchpad
A cursor swipe can use the whole keyboard, and the other keys pause

Once a spacebar swipe starts moving the cursor, the whole keyboard becomes its touchpad. The keys dim, and touching them with another finger types nothing until you lift. With Keep moving while held on, the cursor keeps going when your finger reaches either side of the keyboard rather than the end of the spacebar. Your finger can always leave the spacebar during a swipe; this setting stops the other keys from reacting while it does. This setting is off by default.
Move the cursor directly
Place the cursor instead of pressing arrow keys

A spacebar swipe normally moves the cursor by pressing the left and right arrow keys, the way a hardware keyboard would. Some search boxes read an arrow key as a step through their suggestions, and some file managers put the cursor back at the start of the name after one. With this setting on, the swipe places the cursor directly instead, and no app sees a key press. The app has to tell the keyboard where its cursor is for this to work; when it does not, the arrow keys are used as before. With the 2-D cursor touchpad on, up and down in a one-line field, such as a search box, put the cursor at the start or the end of the text instead of pressing the up and down arrows. In a field with several lines they stay arrow keys, so the cursor follows the app\'s own line wrapping. Selection mode and a held shift always use the arrow keys, which is how they stretch a selection. This setting is off by default.
Speed up long cursor swipes
The further a spacebar swipe goes, the faster the cursor moves

After a short distance at the normal cursor speed, each character needs less movement. The speed increases until it gets to the top speed, and it stays at that speed while you continue in the same direction. When you go back, the speed starts again at the normal speed, so you can correct an overshoot accurately. With the 2-D cursor touchpad, movement up and down also increases speed in the same way. A short swipe moves one character at a time, as before. This setting is off by default.
Top cursor speed
How fast a long spacebar swipe moves the cursor at its fastest
The value is how many times faster than the normal cursor speed the cursor goes at the end of a long swipe. This setting is 4× by default.
Cursor magnifier
Show the text at the cursor, larger, while a spacebar swipe moves the cursor

The magnifier shows the line of text around the cursor. It goes above the cursor when the app tells the keyboard where the cursor is. If the app does not, it goes above the keyboard. The trackpad tool has a separate setting for this.
A smaller distance moves the cursor faster, so a short spacebar can still cross a long line. A larger one is steadier if your slides tend to overshoot. This setting is 16 dp by default.
Word delete distance
How far you swipe backspace to delete the first word

Later words come off faster than the first on a fixed curve, so this one distance tunes the whole gesture. Raise it if words disappear by accident, lower it if clearing a sentence takes too long a pull. This setting is 72 dp by default.
Character delete distance
How far you swipe backspace for each character

Every character costs the same pull, with no speed up, so the count stays easy to follow. Raise it if letters go by too quickly, lower it if a long correction takes too much room. This setting is 20 dp by default.
Learn a word after
How many times you type a word before autocorrect leaves it alone

The keyboard never corrects a word it has learned from you. That protects your names and slang, but it also means one typo you commit once is protected forever. Raise this to make the keyboard wait until it has seen the word more than once. Suggestions are not affected: a word below this count can still be offered, it is just not shielded from correction. This setting is once by default.
Once
Remember a new word after
How many times you type a word nothing recognises before it is saved

Only words that no dictionary knows are counted. A word already in a dictionary needs one use, not several, because there is nothing in doubt about its spelling. Either way a use only counts once you have moved on and left the word alone, so a word you go back and fix, or a swipe that came out as the wrong word, is never counted. Nothing is saved while you are still typing: the words you left alone are added when you close the keyboard, send the message, or move to another field. Lower this if your own names and slang take too long to stick. Set it to 1 to save every new word after a single use. This setting is 3 by default.
Straight away
Offer corrections it isn\'t sure about
Show a chip for a fix that was close, instead of dropping it

Autocorrect has to be nearly certain before it changes a word on its own, because getting that wrong rewrites what you wrote and you may not notice. Everything just short of certain used to be thrown away, even when it was probably right. With this on, those appear as a chip at the start of the suggestion strip. Tap it to apply the fix, or carry on typing and it goes away. A correction you have already undone once is never offered. On by default, and it only ever appears where nothing used to happen at all.
Ask before saving new words
Offer a chip instead of counting how often you type the word
Word menu
What pressing and holding a suggested word offers

Press and hold a word on the suggestion strip to open a menu about it. "Edit" is always there: it opens a card that spells, weights and ranks the word, shows where it comes from, and carries the Never suggest, Add and Delete actions, so you can turn those off to keep the menu short. "Add" only appears while you type a word that is not in your personal dictionary, and "Delete" only for a word the keyboard can forget. "Synonyms" lists words with the same meaning, and tapping one puts it in place of the word. It appears for English words.
Never suggest
Add
Delete
Synonyms
Synonym sources
Where the word menu looks for synonyms, in order

The keyboard asks the first source that is on. When it has no synonyms for the word, or cannot be reached, the keyboard asks the next one. Drag a source to change the order, and turn off a source to never ask it. Online sources receive only the word you held, and a look-up is not stopped by Data saver, because you ask for it.
Adjust rank changes
What the word card\'s rank controls edit

Learned weight edits the same count the personal dictionary shows: how often the keyboard thinks you typed the word. It cannot push a word below a word list\'s own order, and 0 forgets the word. Rank adjustment keeps a separate up-or-down setting for the word that applies on top of every list, so any word can move either way without changing what the keyboard learned. Both by default, one control under the other.
Learned weight
Changes how often the personal dictionary thinks you typed the word
Rank adjustment
Moves the word up or down the strip, whatever list it comes from
Both
Shows the two controls one under the other
Delete edits imported lists
Deleting a word takes it out of your imported word lists

Deleting a word from the suggestion strip forgets it from your personal dictionary, the waiting room, your rank adjustments and Android\'s dictionary. With this on, a word that is also in a word list you imported is removed from that list\'s file too, so it is gone for good; a word in a downloaded list, which cannot be edited, goes on the blacklist instead. With this off, imported lists are left as you imported them and the word is blacklisted the same way, so it stays hidden until you choose Suggest again.

When a word no dictionary knows is typed, the suggestion strip asks whether to add it. Tap the chip to save the word, or the ✕ to never be asked about it again. Nothing is saved unless you tap. Off by default, because a chip after a word you never think about again gets in the way.
Learn from my fixes
Typos you fix by hand teach autocorrect

When you go back and fix a word by hand, the keyboard remembers what you typed and what you changed it to. Fix the same typo twice and autocorrect makes that fix for you from then on. After one fix it offers the fix on the strip instead. The keyboard also learns the slip behind each fix, such as hitting 3 for e or b for the space bar, so the same slip in other words is understood. Undo a learned fix and the keyboard stops making it. A word that is itself a real word, like form for from, only changes after three fixes and when the words around it agree.
Learned corrections
Fixes you taught the keyboard, and the slips it has noticed
Nothing learned yet. Fix a typo by hand and the pair appears here once the text settles.
No learned corrections match \"%1$s\"
Fixes you taught
Forget the fix of %1$s
Forget all learned corrections

resources.string: Every fix you taught and every slip the keyboard noticed is forgotten. Learned words and undone corrections are not affected.
Slips the keyboard has noticed
How your fixes were made, letter by letter. Autocorrect treats these slips as likely for you, so the same slip in a word you never fixed is still understood.
%1$s typed instead of %2$s
%1$s left out
An extra %1$s
%1$s and %2$s swapped
%1$s typed instead of space
A space left out
Mistype tolerance
How far into a neighbouring key a tap may land and still count as a slip

Every tap is read against where it landed, not only against the key it hit, so a tap near the edge of a key can still be read as the key next to it. This sets how generous that reading is. Above 100%, a tap well inside a neighbouring key is still a likely slip, which suits fast or hectic typing and big fingers. Below 100%, the key you hit is trusted more, which suits careful typing. It changes which words the strip offers and what autocorrect picks. The default is 100%.
Learn where my taps land
Words you keep teach the keyboard how you miss each key when tapping

Nobody taps the exact middle of every key. With this on, every word you type and leave standing records where your finger landed on each letter, and later taps are read against keys moved to match. A slip toward a neighbouring key is then corrected the way you actually make it. Swipes have their own version of this under Glide typing. Turn it off to freeze what has been learned, or use Forget below to start over.
Forget where my taps land
Forget learned tap positions?
Taps go back to being read against the keys exactly as drawn, and learning starts again from your next word. Learned words and corrections are not affected.
Words per key
How many words one key can carry, stacked

One word per key is what the BlackBerry and Octopus keyboards drew, and it is all a phone-sized key has room for. On a tablet the keys are tall enough for two or three, stacked away from the key with the likeliest word nearest it. A flick up takes the nearest word; a tap takes the word you touch. How many words still caps the whole keyboard.
